idiom_name: guarded UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ? + sqlite3_changes() / PQcmdTuples()
implementation_notes: C has no ORM or concurrency-token machinery, so the pattern is the SQL guard itself: read the version column with the record, and at commit run UPDATE t SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ? inside one system transaction, deciding the outcome from the affected-row count - sqlite3_changes()/sqlite3_changes64() on SQLite, PQcmdTuples() or an explicit RETURNING clause on PostgreSQL. The classic structure (validator object, session) is replaced by the conditional statement plus an explicit conflict branch; there is no simpler local idiom that keeps the guarantee, because only the database can evaluate the predicate and the write atomically.
pitfalls: sqlite3_changes() reports the most recent INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on that connection and is unpredictable if the connection is used from another thread while it is read - check the count immediately, on the same connection.
Reading the version and updating in two separate transactions destroys the guarantee; both must be inside one system transaction (BEGIN IMMEDIATE where the engine needs the write lock early).
PQcmdTuples() returns a string and is only valid after INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MOVE/FETCH; an explicit RETURNING id gives an unambiguous result and avoids parsing command tags.
